newsitem.title: USA: US stocks to open trace lower after roaring week.
newsitem.headline: US stocks to open trace lower after roaring week.

text.p: U.S. stocks were indicated a trace lower for the opening of trading on Monday as many investors were seen cashing in on their profits from last week while others take the Veterans Day Holiday off.
Last week, the Dow Industrials closed up 198 to about 6220, capping off the second best week ever for the average.
The Standard & Poor's December futures contract was off 0.3 to 733.95. The bond market is closed for the holiday.
"It should be a little lower at the opening. It will be a very quiet day because of the holiday," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities.
Banks, government offices, and the Treasury markets are closed for the observance of Veterans Day. No economic data is due today because of the holiday.
On top of its weekly gains, the Dow stormed to its third consecutive all-time high finish on Friday, closing up 14.
"The question is, will the momentum continue?," he asked, noting that weak market breadth at the end of last week pointed towards a deceleration in stocks.
"The Dow held up, but the broader market was not as great. I wouldn't be surprised if we saw some profit-taking today," Wachtel said.
Last week, the Nasdaq rose 3.37 to 1257.51, less than a point away from its all-time closing high, but analysts noted that decliners led advancers by a narrow margin.
Tokyo stocks settled lower, with their drop eating away at the huge gains posted late last week. The 225-issue Nikkei average fell 136 to land at 21,065, pulled lower by futures.
The key British FTSE 100 fell modestly, off 6.4 to 3904, anticipating a weak Dow opening.

The dollar was steady with a softer bias against the mark in European trading but extended its dip against the yen. Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara said his country's foreign exchange policy was unchanged.

Remarks by Sakakibara, known as "Mr. Yen" and credited with bringing the yen down against the dollar, last week sent the dollar into a tailspin as investors perceived the Group of Three strong dollar policy might be ending.

Before the opening bell, two separate billion-dollar mergers were announced. Drug wholesaler Bergen Brunswig Corp said it will merge with IVAX Corp in a $1.65 billion stock swap giving IVAX shareholders about $13.75 per share of stock in the combined company, less than IVAX's Friday closing price of 15-3/4. Bergen Brunswig shares closed at 32-3/4, up 3/8.
HFS Inc and PHH Corp said they would merge in a $1.7 billion deal that values each share of PHH at $49.50 each, a rich premium above its Friday closing price of 30-3/4.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says Conrail holders may be riled by CSX Corp's move to derail Norfolk Southern Corp's offer for Conrail.
